title: ICH E6(R3) vs. E6(R2): Changes to Sponsor Responsibilities
summary: ICH E6(R2) vs. E6(R3) sponsor obligations: quality management, risk-proportionate monitoring, digital data governance, and service-provider oversight.
body_text: Sponsor responsibilities under ICH E6(R3) versus E6(R2): what changed The headline change: a principles-plus-annexes architecture The single most consequential change for sponsors is structural. E6(R3) is organised around overarching Principles plus Annexes rather than one static list of GCP instructions. The Principles and Annex 1 are intended to reflect and replace the content and scope of E6(R2), while Annex 2 is added for non-traditional trials 84 . The consolidated contents confirm this layout: Introduction, Principles of ICH GCP, Annex 1, and Annex 2 83 , and the guideline states additional annexes may be developed to address emerging innovations 76 . Two cross-cutting design choices flow from this and reshape how every sponsor obligation is read: Media-neutral and technology-agnostic. The guideline is "intended to be media neutral to enable the use of different technologies," and the Principles are "designed to be flexible and applicable to a broad range of clinical trials" 76 . Technology use should be adapted to participant characteristics and the specific trial design, with digital health technologies such as wearables and sensors given as examples 76 . Fit-for-purpose and proportionate as an operating rule. GCP should be tailored to the trial design and the technologies used, and a proportionate, risk-based approach supports evolving designs without compromising participant rights, safety, well-being, or reliability of results 67 68 . The principles "may be satisfied using differing approaches" and applied to fit the trial's purpose 76 . For sponsors, this means the R3 obligations are outcome-based expectations to be scaled to trial risk and complexity, rather than a fixed checklist tied to paper-era processes. Sponsor responsibility changes by domain 1. Quality management and quality by design E6(R3) makes quality management an explicit, structured sponsor responsibility built on quality by design. Under section 3.10 the sponsor must implement an appropriate quality management system across all stages of the trial and adopt a proportionate, risk-based approach that incorporates quality into the design of the trial and prospectively identifies critical-to-quality (CtQ) factors, the attributes likely to have a meaningful impact on participant rights, safety and well-being and on reliability of results 154 . Quality is to be built into scientific and operational design rather than inspected in afterward, with CtQ factors identified prospectively (section 6.2) 158 159 . The range and extent of oversight measures should be fit for purpose and tailored to trial complexity and risk 154 155 . This codifies, as sponsor duties, the quality-by-design and CtQ concepts that were not part of the original core GCP model. 2. Risk management as a defined lifecycle R3 sets out a full risk-management cycle the sponsor must run, section by section under 3.10.1 110 111 : 3.10.1.1 Risk identification: identify risks to CtQ factors before initiation and throughout conduct, considering the processes and systems used, including computerised systems, consent, randomisation, blinding, IMP administration, data handling, and service-provider activities 110 111 . 3.10.1.2 Risk evaluation: assess risks and existing controls by likelihood, detectability, and impact on participant protection and result reliability 110 111 . 3.10.1.3 Risk control: apply proportionate controls, and where relevant set pre-specified acceptable ranges such as quality tolerance limits at the trial level; if exceeded, evaluate whether there is a systemic issue 110 111 . 3.10.1.4 Risk communication: document and communicate risks and mitigations to those who must act on them 110 111 . 3.10.1.5 Risk review: periodically review controls to confirm they remain effective, accounting for emerging knowledge 152 153 . 3.10.1.6 Risk reporting: summarise and report important quality issues, including exceeded acceptable ranges and remedial actions, in the clinical trial report 152 153 . 3. Oversight of service providers and delegated duties R3 tightens and clarifies the sponsor's accountability when work is outsourced. Any trial-related activity transferred to a service provider must be documented in an agreement, and anything not specifically transferred remains the sponsor's responsibility (3.6.4) 59 60 . The sponsor may transfer any or all activities, but ultimate responsibility for participant rights, safety and well-being and for data reliability stays with the sponsor (3.6.6) 59 60 . The sponsor must assess suitability and select providers (3.6.7), provide the protocol and documents needed and have access to SOPs and performance metrics for selection and oversight (3.6.7 to 3.6.8), and ensure appropriate oversight of important activities including those further subcontracted (3.6.9) 59 60 . Service-provider activities must be conducted per relevant GCP (3.6.10), and providers must report incidents that could affect participant safety or results (3.6.6) 59 60 . Where the sponsor arranges activities that fall under the investigator's responsibility, it must ensure the provider is suitable, while the investigator retains oversight of that provider (3.8) 65 66 . 4. Monitoring: risk-based and centralised, by design R3 frames monitoring as a risk-based activity rather than a default of exhaustive on-site source data verification. The sponsor determines the extent and nature of monitoring from identified risks, considering objective, design, complexity, blinding, participant numbers, the IMP, current safety knowledge, and endpoints (3.11.4.1) 106 . Monitoring may be on-site and/or remote, and frequency is set and modified using accumulating knowledge 106 . Centralised monitoring (3.11.4.2), an evaluation of accumulated data by qualified sponsor staff, can complement and reduce site monitoring or stand alone, and can target site selection and processes 106 . The sponsor develops a monitoring plan (3.11.4.3) tailored to safety, data-quality and reliability risks, describing the strategy, activities of all parties, methods and tools and their rationale, giving particular attention to participant safety and endpoints, and referencing the sponsor's policies and procedures 106 . 5. Data governance and computerised systems R3 introduces a dedicated data-governance framework as a sponsor responsibility spanning the full data life cycle. The sponsor should ensure systems and processes are designed proportionate to risks to participants and to reliability, and documented, covering confidentiality of participant data, fit-for-purpose management of computerised systems, safeguarding essential elements such as randomisation, dose adjustments and blinding, and supporting key decisions such as data finalisation before analysis, unblinding, allocation to analysis sets, design changes, and IDMC activities (section 4) 104 105 . The data life cycle is enumerated (4.2.1 to 4.2.8: capture, metadata and audit trails, review, corrections, transfer/migration, finalisation, retention and access, destruction) 104 105 , and computerised systems carry their own subsections (4.3.1 to 4.3.8: procedures, training, security, validation, release, failure, technical support, user management) 102 103 . This structured, life-cycle treatment of data integrity and computerised-system governance is a substantive expansion of the sponsor's explicit duties. 6. Safety assessment and reporting R3 keeps the sponsor responsible for ongoing safety evaluation and organises the obligations under section 3.13. The sponsor is responsible for ongoing safety evaluation of the IMP, with the Investigator's Brochure (or current scientific information) as the basis of assessment, and must aggregate and review safety information in a timely way, including events before IMP administration such as during screening, and update the protocol, IB, consent materials and related documents as needed (3.13.1) 135 . Reporting duties (3.13.2) include submitting safety updates and periodic reports, expediting SUSARs to authorities per applicable requirements and ICH E2A, judging expectedness against the reference safety information, reporting to investigators and IRBs/IECs with appropriate urgency, reporting urgent safety issues without undue delay, and using alternative reporting arrangements only where prospectively agreed with authorities and described in the protocol 133 134 . Section 3.13.3 requires prompt action on immediate hazards, determination of causes, and remedial action 133 134 . 7. Investigational product management Under section 3.16-related provisions, the sponsor supplies the IMP to investigators/institutions (and, where appropriate and permitted, directly to participants), only after required IRB/IEC and regulatory approval, with safeguards for product integrity, protocol use and participant safety 116 . The sponsor ensures handling and storage instructions covering receipt, handling, storage, dispensing, retrieval of unused product, and return or authorised disposition 116 ; supports blinding, including a process to prevent and detect inappropriate unblinding and a mechanism for rapid emergency identification while protecting other assignments 116 ; and, for significant formulation changes, has the supporting studies (for example stability, dissolution, bioavailability) before use 116 . Products should be managed per specifications and protocol, with processes for handling, shipping, storage, dispensing, return, and destruction or disposal 121 122 . 8. Protocol, trial design and participant engagement R3 pushes design quality and feasibility onto the sponsor's plate. The protocol should be clear, concise and operationally feasible, minimise unnecessary complexity, and mitigate or eliminate important risks, incorporating input from relevant interested parties where appropriate (Appendix B) 100 101 . The sponsor must ensure design, conduct and the data generated are of sufficient quality to support reliable results and sound decisions, and provide the protocol and an up-to-date Investigator's Brochure to potential investigators with sufficient review time (3.7 and 3.9) 95 97 . R3 also introduces explicit sponsor-facing language on early patient and community engagement: involving patients and advocacy groups early can help refine the design, address the logistics of participation, and assess suitability of digital health technologies used in decentralised elements (3.1.1) 87 . 9. Non-traditional trials: Annex 2 (new) Annex 2 has no counterpart in E6(R2). It was added because of increased use of varied operational approaches, design elements and data sources, and it addresses trials with decentralised elements, pragmatic elements, and/or real-world data 67 68 . Decentralised elements are activities conducted outside the investigator's location (home visits, local healthcare centres, mobile units, remote video, and DHTs for visits, procedures and data collection); pragmatic elements integrate usual clinical practice, such as simplified protocols and streamlined data collection 67 68 . Annex 2 defines RWD as patient health-status data from sources outside trials (EHRs, registries, claims), distinguishes primary collection from secondary use, and requires such data to be fit for purpose when used for endpoints or as external controls 74 75 . Annex 2 is expressly not comprehensive and not an endorsement of any specific methodology 67 68 . How to read these changes as a sponsor The net effect is a shift from prescriptive, process-level GCP to an accountability model where the sponsor designs quality in, runs a documented risk-management cycle, and scales oversight, monitoring, and data governance to trial-specific risk, all in a technology-neutral frame that explicitly accommodates decentralised and real-world-data trials 76 67 68 84 . The specific sponsor clauses have been reorganised and, in several areas (quality by design, the risk cycle, data governance and computerised systems, and Annex 2), materially expanded relative to the original core GCP model. Limitations This analysis is grounded in the E6(R3) documents available in the ICH corpus. The full E6(R2) consolidated text is not present in this dataset, so the change statements rely on E6(R3)'s own description of what it replaced (Principles plus Annex 1 reflecting and replacing R2, Annex 2 as new) rather than a line-by-line diff against the R2 source 84 83 . For a clause-level comparison of any single requirement, confirm the corresponding E6(R2) wording against the R2 document directly.

title: Bühler and Entocycle partner to deliver end-to-end technology solutions to insect farms
summary: Bühler and Entocycle partner to deliver end-to-end technology solutions to insect farms
body_text: Bühler, one of the world’s leading processing technology groups, and Entocycle, the UK’s leading insect technology company, have joined forces to drive the adoption of large-scale black soldier fly (BSF) farms. The companies will provide solutions and expertise to serve customers in this segment, covering the multiple steps of the journey, from concept and basic engineering to execution of BSF facilities worldwide. The non-exclusive partnership creates a highly complementary offering, with Entocycle delivering proprietary breeding technology and Bühler bringing proven industrial-scale technologies in feedstock processing, larvae rearing, and product processing. One of the challenges of the highly promising, emerging insect industry has been ensuring a steady supply of young larvae at an industrial scale. “While the pioneers in this industry had to develop their own technology out of necessity to ensure a robust BSF breeding, companies now venturing into this industry will be able to rely on a proven and scalable solution,” says Andreas Baumann, Head of Market Segment Insect Technology at Bühler. Although there are specialized breeding service companies in certain regions, in large parts of the world, there is no alternative to having an in-house breeding operation. With this partnership, Bühler and Entocycle address this challenge by offering scalable end-to-end solutions that significantly reduce the time to market for companies building an insect facility. During the last ten years, Bühler has been developing its capabilities in the insect protein industry and has already completed a number of relevant projects in the field. In 2019, Bühler supported Protix in the realisation of the world’s first commercial BSF plant in the Netherlands and this year Bühler delivered Agronutris’ first industrial BSF plant in France. “We are incredibly proud to partner with Bühler, a company with 163 years of illustrious history. Our team is really excited to work with Andreas Baumann and his team to deliver large-scale BSF facilities around the world and make the impact that we know BSF farming can make in creating a more sustainable and efficient global food system,” says Keiran Whitaker, Founder and CEO of Entocycle. “The industrial use of BSF is rapidly gaining traction among businesses seeking alternative feed protein sources and more sustainable practices. To accelerate scaling this industry, we must contribute to lowering the hurdles for companies to enter this business,” says Andreas Baumann. “That is why we are very pleased to cooperate with the Entocycle team in future projects, as they share the same philosophy as Bühler in ensuring the quality and reliability of their solutions.” “It’s going to be a great partnership, not only in the way that our businesses and teams complement one another in terms of respective skill sets and experience but also in the strong alignment of values around building a better and more sustainable world,” says Matthew Simmonds, Managing Director of Entocycle.

title: How a College Student Turned Hinge Dates Into Viral Startup Marketing
summary: Learn the crazy story of how Eunice Lai became a startup CMO by doing the opposite of what everyone else was doing.
body_text: The secret to blowing up your startup isn't your product, your funding, or your connections. It might just be finding the right college student who treats dating apps…like user acquisition funnels? In today's recap of our podcast interview, Joseph sat down with Eunice Lai, a 20-year-old college student who became the CMO of Series, a viral startup. Her track record includes over 3 million impressions across LinkedIn and Twitter, three viral launch videos, and some truly unconventional marketing tactics. If you haven't watched the full interview yet, I'd recommend checking it out below: But as always, here's my breakdown of the key points: The Hinge strategy that broke "Tech Twitter" When Eunice joined the startup world this summer, she knew X was where the conversations happened. Her first post got 20 likes, which sounds like nothing, but as she puts it, "that's a lot more than most people on X because most people stay in one, two, three likes jail." She started with the typical "build in public" approach everyone was doing. So instead, she tried something different. When she was in New York for her first summer, she hooped on Hinge. In her bio, she listed "startup" as her job. When matches asked what kind of startup she worked at, instead of giving a straight answer, she'd drop playful hints like "the first AI social network." Her breakthrough came from a real interaction. A guy searched her up after matching and messaged "Series is cool." Her response? "So you're trying to become a user." She tweeted the exchange and named him "Jason [Hinge]" in the screenshot. People found the idea of reducing a date to a potential conversion both absurd and hilarious. That's when the tweet went viral. But here's the part that actually surprised me, she actually went on the date! And…she actually converted him! She walked him through the entire onboarding process and watched him become a user in real time. "I didn't want it to be too overt," she explains. "We had a really good time. We talked about life and ambitions before I popped the question at the end." The user conversion question, that is. So, how does this relate to tech marketing? Let's get to that part next. Doing the opposite and why calm content converts Eunice's approach to content is deceptively simple: "Do the opposite of what people are doing right now." I think her Hinge setup embodies that well, too. And that's where her inspiration came from. Aside from Hinge, Her Instagram reels are a perfect example. While everyone was making vertical videos with loud text and rage-bait hooks, she posted a horizontal video of herself just talking for 90 seconds. The view count wasn't massive at 35,000, but it converted between 200 and 250 followers. That's an incredibly high conversion rate for Instagram. So, why did it work? I think the main reason was because it was different (true to her marketing and posting ethos). People scrolling through endless vertical content suddenly saw something calm and authentic. It felt like connecting with a real person instead of consuming another algorithm-optimized piece of content. She also pointed out something that more creators are discovering: you have to full send the persona. "If you only put a foot in the door, people are going to be able to tell that maybe this is not your true self and you're trying too hard. But if you really put your entire brand into it, the smart people realize you know what you're doing and they play along with it." The trick is taking one small aspect of your personality that's genuinely true and playing it up to the max. On the internet, you're in a crowd of a hundred people, so you have to amplify yourself to stand out. The campaign that pulled 2,500 applications So, with a good format and ideas that worked, she started using these ideas at Series. For Series, Eunice ran a campaign around their Hamptons event that showcased how social proof compounds. She had interns compete for a spot in a reality TV-style show about startups. The challenge format tapped into something she'd identified about viral content: people love the day-by-day journey. They want to see if you can actually achieve your goal, so they follow along. They made a LinkedIn post and job listing about it. Over 2,500 people applied. Initially, the show only had 12 spots, but Eunice saw an opportunity. Why waste all that interest? She turned it into a competition where 150 people joined the "race to the Hamptons." One of the final challenges was to invite as many people as possible. The first-place person invited 120 people in a single day. She noticed something interesting about LinkedIn specifically. Students don't usually like to post there, but once one or two people started sharing about the campaign, everyone became comfortable doing the same. Within two days, over a hundred interns had posted banners and paragraphs about what entrepreneurship meant to them. "LinkedIn is such an undervalued channel for students," she says. "I would say the highest value followers you can have are probably LinkedIn followers." What founders get wrong when hiring creators When startup founders reach out to Eunice now, she can immediately tell who's put thought into their approach and who hasn't. The bad pitches are the ones that just say "I want my own version of a TV show" because they saw something go viral. They're looking to her for all the ideas without bringing anything to the table themselves. There has to be genuine ideas coming from both sides. The good pitches, though, come from founders who understand their target audience and have at least a hypothesis about what might resonate. "I think it's very clear when a founder isn't putting thought into how they want to approach it," she explains. The pitch that works sounds more like: "My target audience is this, I think they might appreciate a campaign like this because they love watching Love Island, so let's see how we can spin up our own version." That kind of thinking reflects on the product itself. She also emphasizes that big creators who are good at building their own brand don't necessarily know how to build someone else's. That point resonated with me, I've tried a little bit of influencer reach-out myself. Conventional wisdom would usually lead you to thinking that the bigger the influencer, the better the results. So, Eunice trained herself specifically to make content from the perspective of a company or brand, telling their story rather than her own. That's a different skill set than just having a lot of followers. Managing creative talent without killing creativity For startup founders wondering how to work with content creators, Eunice's advice is simple: let them cook! The more you prescribe formulas and detailed requirements, the less creative people feel. Creative burnout is real, especially when you're trying to generate fresh stories from a single concept. If you put more pressure on them with strict quantitative KPIs, they won't execute as well as they could. You can't set a goal like "this video has to get a million likes." Even creators with a million followers can't guarantee that. Virality is part strategy, part luck. And, that's something we see over and over with these interviews we do. Instead, focus on qualitative goals. Does the content reflect your brand identity? Are users taking away the right information? You can set quantitative goals once you have actual data points to work with, but in the beginning, make sure your marketing person understands who the user is and what the goals are. Then let them figure out how to get there. Trust them. That's how you get the best work. Wrapping up Eunice represents something I think a lot of founders are starting to realize. The social media intern isn't at the bottom of the totem pole anymore. In many ways, they've become the most important person for distribution. The tables have completely turned. Her success comes from recognizing that behind every viral moment is a real human story. By staying authentic while playing with the conventions of social media, she's created content that doesn't just get views but builds community. For startup founders, the lesson is clear: find people who can turn boring topics into engaging stories, give them the freedom to experiment, and focus on building relationships rather than just chasing metrics. Look for potential over follower count. Someone who's built accounts from the ground up understands engagement mechanics in ways that people who inherited large followings might not.
